title: The Cedar Forest: Huwawa's Terror
subtitle: The fame-quest that costs more than it earns

learningObjectives.text: Why do they go to the Cedar Forest?

terror.work: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
terror.author: Anonymous
terror.translator: Morris Jastrow and Albert T. Clay
terror.locator: Yale Tablet · Column IV; Yale Tablet · Column IV, normalized characters 0-1009
terror.excerpt: To keep safe [the cedar forest], [Enlil has decreed for it] seven-fold terror." Gish [opened] his mouth and spoke to [Enkidu]: "Whoever, my friend, overcomes (?) [terror(?)], it is well (for him) with Shamash for the length of [his days]. Mankind will speak of it at the gates. Wherever terror is to be faced, Thou, forsooth, art in fear of death. Thy prowess lacks strength. I will go before thee. Though thy mouth calls to me; "thou art afraid to approach." If I fall, I will establish my name. Gish, the corpse(?) of Huwawa, the terrible one, has snatched (?) from the time that My offspring was born in ...... The lion restrained (?) thee, all of which thou knowest. ........................ .............. thee and ................ open (?) ........ like a shepherd(?) ..... [When thou callest to me], thou afflictest my heart. I am determined [to enter] the cedar forest. I will, indeed, establish my name. [The work(?)], my friend, to the artisans I will entrust. [Weapons(?)] let them mould before us.
terror.note: Verbatim translation from the named Old Babylonian tablet witness in this edited edition. Brackets and question marks signal textual restoration or uncertainty.

narrativeBlocks.title: A name worth having
narrativeBlocks.body: Gilgamesh wants the one thing immortality can't give: a name that outlasts him. The target is Huwawa — the monstrous guardian of the gods' Cedar Forest, whose roar alone can kill.

narrativeBlocks.title: Enkidu's foreboding
narrativeBlocks.body: Enkidu knows the guardian — he met Huwawa in his wild days — and warns that the giant's terror is the real weapon. The dream-omens Gilgamesh interprets as favour keep pulling them forward anyway.

narrativeBlocks.title: The terror defeated
narrativeBlocks.body: They reach the forest and do the deed — Huwawa is brought down by their combined strength and the god Shamash's favour. The fame-quest succeeds.

narrativeBlocks.title: And the gods notice
narrativeBlocks.body: But Huwawa was APPOINTED guardian by the gods — killing him is sacrilege as well as heroism. The victory becomes the charge-sheet: the divine council decides one of the two friends must pay.

narrativeBlocks.title: The beginning of the grief
narrativeBlocks.body: The bill comes due in the next tablets: Enkidu sickens and dies. The fame-quest is the hinge — Gilgamesh gets his name and loses the person who made it bearable.

quiz.prompt: Why do Gilgamesh and Enkidu go to the Cedar Forest?

choices.text: For fame — Gilgamesh wants a name that outlasts him, and Huwawa's defeat is the prize
To fulfill a vow to Shamhat

quiz.explanation: The quest is glory-seeking — and the price is far higher than either expects.

quiz.prompt: What is the cost of killing Huwawa?

choices.text: The gods mark it sacrilege — the council decides a life must pay, and Enkidu sickens and dies

quiz.explanation: The 'victory' is the bill — Enkidu's death begins the grief that drives the epic's second half.
